content: The review authors evaluated the risk of bias (RoB) in individual studies when interpreting and discussing the results of the review. They also provided a satisfactory explanation for any heterogeneity observed in the review findings. If quantitative synthesis was performed, the authors investigated publication bias (e.g., small study bias) and discussed its potential impact on the review results. Additionally, the authors disclosed any potential conflicts of interest, including funding sources for conducting the review. The AMSTAR 2 tool, developed by Shea et al. in 2017, is a critical appraisal tool designed for systematic reviews that include randomized or non-randomized studies of healthcare interventions, or both. Sedentary Behavior and All-Cause Mortality 1. Berger et al. (2019): This review included three prospective cohort studies with 277,763 participants. The studies primarily relied on self-reported sedentary behavior, with one study combining self-reports and job title assignments. The mean follow-up time was not reported. The evidence showed a serious risk of bias, inconsistency, and indirectness, but no serious imprecision. The findings indicated very low certainty of evidence. 2. Del Pozo-Cruz et al. (2018): This review analyzed three prospective cohort studies with 12,108 participants. The review reported that replacing 30 minutes of sedentary time with light-intensity physical activity (LIPA) or moderate-to-vigorous physical activity (MVPA) was associated with a significantly lower risk of all-cause mortality. However, the certainty of evidence was low due to serious inconsistency and imprecision. 3. Ekelund et al. (2018): This review included 11 prospective cohort studies with 888,327 participants. It found a dose-response relationship between sitting time and all-cause mortality. Sitting time was categorized into four groups (<4 hours/day, 4–6 hours/day, 6–8 hours/day, and >8 hours/day). The highest sitting time group (>8 hours/day) had significantly increased mortality risk compared to the reference group (<4 hours/day). However, no clear dose-response association was observed in other quartiles of physical activity (PA). The certainty of evidence was high. 4. Ku et al. (2018): This review analyzed 19 prospective cohort studies with 1,250,482 participants. Longer follow-up studies showed weaker associations between daily sedentary time and mortality risks. The certainty of evidence was low due to serious inconsistency and indirectness. 5. Ku et al. (2019): This review focused on older adults (>65 years) and included 11 prospective cohort studies with 36,341 participants. The findings suggested that increased sedentary time (>9 hours/day) was associated with higher all-cause mortality risk. The certainty of evidence was moderate. Sedentary Behavior and Cardiovascular Disease (CVD) Mortality 1. Ekelund et al. (2019): This review included eight prospective cohort studies with 36,383 participants. A dose-response relationship was observed, with higher sedentary time significantly associated with increased all-cause mortality. The certainty of evidence was high. 2. Xu et al. (2019): This review analyzed seven prospective cohort studies with 284,161 participants. The findings indicated a dose-response relationship between sedentary activity and all-cause mortality, but the certainty of evidence was low due to limitations in study inclusion and lack of adjustment for light-intensity physical activity (LIPA). Sedentary Behavior and Cancer Mortality 1. Berger et al. (2019): This review included 12 prospective cohort studies with 671,852 participants. Most studies relied on self-reported sedentary behavior, and the mean follow-up time was not reported. No significant associations were found between sitting (e.g., watching TV or at work) and preor post-menopausal breast cancer. The certainty of evidence was very low due to serious risk of bias, inconsistency, and indirectness. Sedentary Behavior and Type 2 Diabetes Incidence 1. Ahmad et al. (2017): This review included one prospective cohort, one case-control, and two cross-sectional studies with 158,964 participants. Greater sedentary time was associated with a higher prevalence of diabetes. The prospective cohort study reported an 84% increased risk of developing diabetes in the highest quartile of sedentary time. The certainty of evidence was moderate. Sedentary Behavior and Adiposity 1. Ahmad et al. (2017): This review included one prospective cohort, one case-control, and 13 cross-sectional studies with 13,395 participants. Thirteen out of 15 studies reported a significant association between higher sedentary time and increased BMI, while two studies found no significant association. The certainty of evidence was very low due to serious risk of bias and imprecision. 2. Del Pozo-Cruz et al. (2018): This review analyzed six cross-sectional studies with 4,774 participants. The findings suggested that replacing sedentary time with MVPA was associated with lower BMI, but the results were not statistically significant after removing one study contributing to heterogeneity. The certainty of evidence was very low. Summary The evidence consistently highlights the association between prolonged sedentary behavior and increased risks of all-cause mortality, cardiovascular disease, type 2 diabetes, and adiposity. However, the certainty of evidence varies across outcomes due to limitations such as risk of bias, inconsistency, and indirectness. High-quality studies are needed to better understand these associations and inform targeted interventions.
